notes.h: Random variables, expectation and the key distributions
notes.body:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. Discrete variables have a probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x). Continuous variables have a density f(x), and probabilities are areas: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ f(x) dx from a to b. The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) works for both.

Moments
- Expectation: E[X] = Σ x·p(x) or ∫ x f(x) dx. It is linear: E[a + bX] = a + bE[X].
- Variance: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])². Var(a + bX) = b²Var(X).
- Covariance: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]; correlation ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σₓσᵧ) lies in [−1, 1].
- Var(aX + bY) = a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y) + 2ab·Cov(X,Y).

Conditional ideas
- Conditional expectation E[Y|X] is a function of X. The law of iterated expectations says E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]]. This underpins regression, which models E[Y|X].
- Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence (e.g. X symmetric about 0 and Y = X²).
- Bayes' rule: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).

Distributions you must know
- Bernoulli(p): mean p, variance p(1 − p). Binomial(n, p): mean np, variance np(1 − p).
- Poisson(λ): counts of rare events; mean and variance both λ.
- Normal N(μ, σ²): standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ. About 68% of mass within ±1σ, 95% within ±1.96σ.
- Chi-squared χ²(k): sum of k squared independent standard normals.
- Student t(k): Z/√(χ²(k)/k); fatter tails than the normal, converging to N(0,1) as k grows.
- F(k₁, k₂): ratio of two independent chi-squareds each divided by its degrees of freedom.

Worked example
A portfolio holds equal weights in assets with standard deviations 0.2 and 0.3 and correlation 0.5. Variance = 0.25(0.04) + 0.25(0.09) + 2(0.25)(0.5)(0.2)(0.3) = 0.0475, so the standard deviation is about 0.218, below the simple average of 0.25. This is diversification in one line.

Exam pitfalls
- Forgetting the covariance term when adding variances, or writing Var(X − Y) = Var(X) − Var(Y). The correct version is Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2Cov(X,Y).
- Treating a density value as a probability; f(x) can exceed 1.
- Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) (the base-rate fallacy).

notes.h: Sampling distributions, estimators and their properties
notes.body:
We observe a sample to learn about population parameters. An estimator is a rule (a function of the sample) such as the sample mean X̄; an estimate is the number it produces in one sample. Because samples vary, an estimator is itself a random variable with a sampling distribution.

Properties of estimators
- Unbiased: E[θ̂] = θ. X̄ is unbiased for μ. The sample variance s² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased for σ²; dividing by n gives a biased estimator (the n − 1 corrects for using X̄ in place of μ).
- Efficiency: among unbiased estimators, prefer the one with smaller variance.
- Mean squared error: MSE = Var(θ̂) + Bias². A slightly biased estimator can have lower MSE.
- Consistency: θ̂ converges in probability to θ as n → ∞. Sufficient conditions: bias and variance both shrink to zero.

Two big theorems
- Law of large numbers: with i.i.d. draws and finite mean, X̄ → μ in probability.
- Central limit theorem: with i.i.d. draws and finite variance, √n(X̄ − μ)/σ converges to N(0,1) whatever the shape of the population. So X̄ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) in large samples.
- Standard error of the mean: σ/√n, estimated by s/√n. Quadrupling n halves the standard error.

Methods of estimation
- Method of moments: set sample moments equal to population moments and solve.
- Maximum likelihood: choose parameter values that make the observed data most probable. Under regularity conditions ML estimators are consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient.
- Least squares: minimise squared deviations; for the mean this gives X̄.

Worked example
A survey of n = 600 finds 42% support a policy. The estimated standard error is √(0.42 × 0.58/600) ≈ 0.0201. By the CLT, the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal, so a 95% interval is roughly 0.42 ± 1.96 × 0.0201, i.e. about 38.1% to 45.9%.

Sample size planning: to estimate a proportion within ±3 points at 95% confidence in the worst case (p = 0.5), you need n ≥ 1.96² × 0.25/0.03² ≈ 1067.1, so round up to n = 1068.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying the CLT makes the data normal. It concerns the distribution of the sample mean, not individual observations.
- Mixing up standard deviation (spread of the data) with standard error (spread of an estimator).
- Assuming unbiasedness implies consistency, or vice versa; neither implies the other in general.
- Ignoring non-random sampling: the CLT does nothing to fix selection bias.

notes.h: Hypothesis tests, p-values and confidence intervals
notes.body:
A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis H₀ (e.g. μ = μ₀) with an alternative H₁ (two-sided μ ≠ μ₀ or one-sided μ > μ₀). We compute a test statistic whose distribution under H₀ is known and ask whether the observed value would be unusual if H₀ were true.

The general recipe
- t = (estimate − hypothesised value)/standard error.
- With small samples from a normal population, use t with n − 1 degrees of freedom; in large samples, N(0,1) is a good approximation.
- Reject H₀ at level α if |t| exceeds the critical value (1.96 for a two-sided 5% test in large samples), or equivalently if the p-value is below α.

Key terms
- Size (α): P(reject H₀ | H₀ true) = Type I error rate.
- Type II error: failing to reject a false H₀; power = 1 − P(Type II). Power rises with sample size, effect size and α, and falls with noise.
- p-value: the probability, computed assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

Confidence intervals
- A 95% CI is estimate ± critical value × SE. Across repeated samples, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true parameter.
- Duality: a two-sided 5% test rejects H₀: θ = θ₀ exactly when θ₀ lies outside the 95% CI.

Worked example (difference in means)
Group A: n = 100, mean 54, variance 144. Group B: n = 120, mean 50, variance 100. SE of the difference = √(144/100 + 100/120) ≈ 1.508. t = 4/1.508 ≈ 2.65, so the two-sided p-value is about 0.008 and we reject equal means at 1% and 5%. The 95% CI is 4 ± 1.96 × 1.508, roughly (1.04, 6.96), which excludes zero, as duality says it must.

Other tests to recognise
- Chi-squared tests for goodness of fit and independence in contingency tables.
- F-tests for comparing variances and, in regression, joint restrictions.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying "we accept H₀". Say "we fail to reject H₀"; absence of evidence is not proof.
- Interpreting a single 95% CI as having a 95% probability of containing θ (in the frequentist framework the interval is random, not θ).
- Equating statistical significance with economic importance: with huge n, trivial effects become significant.
- Running many tests and reporting only significant ones (multiple testing, p-hacking).

The simple regression model is Yᵢ = β₀ + β₁Xᵢ + uᵢ, where u collects everything else that affects Y. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses b₀ and b₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(Yᵢ − b₀ − b₁Xᵢ)².

The OLS formulas
- β̂₁ = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)(Yᵢ − Ȳ)/Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)² = sample Cov(X,Y)/sample Var(X).
- β̂₀ = Ȳ − β̂₁X̄, so the fitted line passes through (X̄, Ȳ).
- Residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with X in the sample.

Goodness of fit
- TSS = ESS + RSS. R² = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS, the share of the sample variation in Y explained by X. In simple regression R² equals the squared sample correlation.

Assumptions for unbiasedness (Gauss–Markov set)
- Linear in parameters; random sampling; variation in X; zero conditional mean E[u|X] = 0.
- Add homoskedasticity, Var(u|X) = σ², and OLS is BLUE: the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov theorem).
- Under homoskedasticity, Var(β̂₁) = σ²/Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)², estimated using s² = RSS/(n − 2).

Interpretation with logs
- Level–level: one unit more X changes Y by β₁ units.
- Log–level (ln Y on X): roughly 100β₁% change in Y per unit of X (exactly 100(e^β₁ − 1)%).
- Level–log: a 1% rise in X changes Y by about β₁/100 units.
- Log–log: β₁ is an elasticity.

Worked example
X = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 (advertising, £000) and Y = 9, 12, 14, 18, 19, 24 (sales, £0000). X̄ = 35, Ȳ = 16, Σxy = 500, Σx² = 1750. So β̂₁ = 500/1750 ≈ 0.286 and β̂₀ = 16 − 0.286 × 35 = 6. RSS = 22/7 ≈ 3.14, TSS = 146, R² ≈ 0.978. s² = 3.14/4 ≈ 0.786, SE(β̂₁) = √(0.786/1750) ≈ 0.0212, t ≈ 13.5.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating a high R² as evidence of causation or of a correctly specified model.
- Saying OLS requires u to be normal for unbiasedness; normality only matters for exact small-sample inference.
- Forgetting that E[u|X] = 0 is the crucial, untestable assumption: residuals are uncorrelated with X by construction, so checking that tells you nothing.
- Extrapolating far outside the range of the observed X.

notes.h: Multiple regression, omitted variables and functional form
notes.body:
Multiple regression, Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + … + βₖXₖ + u, lets us estimate the effect of one regressor holding the others fixed. In matrix form β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y.

Partialling out (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem)
β̂₁ equals the slope from regressing Y on the residuals from a regression of X₁ on all other regressors. So each coefficient uses only the variation in that regressor not explained by the others: this is what "ceteris paribus" means in practice.

Omitted variable bias
If the true model is Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + β₂X₂ + u but we omit X₂, then the short-regression slope has expectation β₁ + β₂δ₁, where δ₁ is the slope from regressing X₂ on X₁. Bias is zero only if β₂ = 0 or X₁ and X₂ are uncorrelated.
- Sign rule: bias has the sign of β₂ × Corr(X₁, X₂).
- Example: wage on education omitting ability. Ability raises wages (β₂ > 0) and correlates positively with schooling, so the return to education is biased upward.

Multicollinearity
- Perfect collinearity (e.g. including every category dummy plus an intercept, the dummy variable trap) makes OLS impossible.
- High but imperfect collinearity does not bias OLS; it inflates standard errors. The variance inflation factor VIFⱼ = 1/(1 − Rⱼ²).

Goodness of fit
- R² never falls when a regressor is added. Adjusted R̄² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1) penalises extra regressors.
- Example: R² = 0.40, n = 50, k = 4 gives R̄² = 1 − 0.6 × 49/45 ≈ 0.347.

Functional form tools
- Dummy variables shift the intercept; interaction terms (D × X) let slopes differ by group.
- Quadratics capture diminishing effects: with Y = β₀ + β₁X + β₂X², the marginal effect is β₁ + 2β₂X and the turning point is at X = −β₁/(2β₂).
- Ramsey RESET test adds powers of fitted values to check for neglected nonlinearity.

Exam pitfalls
- Adding "bad controls" that are themselves outcomes of the treatment, which can create bias rather than remove it.
- Interpreting a coefficient on X when X also appears in an interaction or quadratic without evaluating the full marginal effect.
- Dropping a variable because it is insignificant when theory says it belongs and it is correlated with the regressor of interest.
- Thinking multicollinearity causes bias.

notes.h: Inference in regression and diagnostic testing
notes.body:
To test hypotheses about β we need the sampling distribution of β̂. Under the classical assumptions plus normal errors, t = (β̂ⱼ − βⱼ⁰)/SE(β̂ⱼ) follows t with n − k − 1 degrees of freedom. In large samples the CLT gives approximate normality without normal errors.

Joint hypotheses: the F-test
- To test q restrictions (e.g. β₂ = β₃ = 0), compare restricted and unrestricted models: F = [(RSSᵣ − RSSᵤ)/q]/[RSSᵤ/(n − k − 1)].
- The R² form is equivalent when the dependent variable is the same.
- Individually insignificant variables can be jointly significant, especially when collinear.

Worked example
n = 120, unrestricted model with k = 5 regressors has RSSᵤ = 480; dropping two regressors gives RSSᵣ = 520. F = (40/2)/(480/114) ≈ 4.75. The 5% critical value of F(2, 114) is about 3.08, so we reject the null that both coefficients are zero (p ≈ 0.01).

Heteroskedasticity
- Var(u|X) depends on X. OLS stays unbiased and consistent but the usual standard errors are wrong and OLS is no longer BLUE.
- Detect: Breusch–Pagan (regress squared residuals on regressors; LM = nR² ~ χ²(k)) or White's test (adds squares and cross-products).
- Fix: heteroskedasticity-robust (White/Eicker–Huber) standard errors, or weighted least squares if the form is known.

Serial correlation (time series)
- Errors correlated over time; again OLS is unbiased under strict exogeneity, but standard errors are wrong.
- Detect: Durbin–Watson (DW ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂), so near 2 means no first-order autocorrelation) or Breusch–Godfrey, which also works with lagged dependent variables.
- Fix: Newey–West (HAC) standard errors, or model the dynamics.

Other diagnostics
- Normality of residuals: Jarque–Bera (uses skewness and kurtosis).
- Structural breaks: Chow test.
- Specification: RESET.
- Influential points: leverage and Cook's distance.

Exam pitfalls
- Claiming heteroskedasticity biases the coefficients. It biases the standard errors.
- Using Durbin–Watson when a lagged dependent variable is a regressor (it is biased towards 2; use Breusch–Godfrey).
- Using the R² version of the F-test when the dependent variable differs between models.
- Concluding "the model is fine" because diagnostics do not reject; tests have limited power.

A regressor is endogenous when it is correlated with the error term, so E[u|X] ≠ 0 and OLS is biased and inconsistent. Three main sources:
- Omitted variables correlated with X (e.g. ability in a wage equation).
- Measurement error in X: classical error biases the slope towards zero (attenuation bias). Error in Y only reduces precision.
- Simultaneity: X and Y determined jointly, as with price and quantity in supply and demand.

Instrumental variables
An instrument Z must satisfy:
- Relevance: Cov(Z, X) ≠ 0. Testable from the first stage.
- Exogeneity (exclusion): Cov(Z, u) = 0, so Z affects Y only through X. Not directly testable with one instrument; it must be argued.

With one instrument and one endogenous regressor, β̂_IV = Cov(Z,Y)/Cov(Z,X): the reduced-form effect of Z on Y divided by the first-stage effect of Z on X.

Two-stage least squares (2SLS)
- Stage 1: regress X on Z and the exogenous controls; save fitted values X̂.
- Stage 2: regress Y on X̂ and the controls.
- Run it as one command: manual second-stage standard errors are wrong.

Diagnostics
- Weak instruments: if the first stage is weak, 2SLS is biased towards OLS and inference is unreliable. A common rule of thumb (Staiger and Stock, 1997) flags a first-stage F below 10; more recent work argues for stricter thresholds.
- Overidentification (Sargan/Hansen J): with more instruments than endogenous regressors, tests whether instruments agree. Rejection casts doubt on at least one; non-rejection does not prove validity.
- Durbin–Wu–Hausman test compares OLS and IV to test for endogeneity.

Classic applications
- Angrist and Krueger (1991): quarter of birth as an instrument for schooling, using compulsory schooling laws. Bound, Jaeger and Baker (1995) showed the weak-instrument problems with this design.
- Card (1995): proximity to a college as an instrument for education.

Worked example
The reduced form shows that living near a college raises log wages by 0.042; the first stage shows it raises schooling by 0.32 years. β̂_IV = 0.042/0.32 ≈ 0.131, about a 13% return per year of schooling.

Interpretation
With heterogeneous effects, IV estimates a local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers, those whose treatment is shifted by the instrument (Imbens and Angrist, 1994).

Exam pitfalls
- Testing exogeneity by regressing Y on Z (Z should affect Y, through X).
- Assuming IV is always better: with a weak or invalid instrument it can be worse than OLS.
- Ignoring that LATE may not generalise to the whole population.

Panel data
Panel data follow the same units i over time t. The model Yᵢₜ = βXᵢₜ + αᵢ + uᵢₜ includes an unobserved, time-invariant individual effect αᵢ.
- Pooled OLS is biased if αᵢ is correlated with X.
- First differences: ΔYᵢₜ = βΔXᵢₜ + Δuᵢₜ removes αᵢ.
- Fixed effects (within) estimator: demean each variable by its unit average; equivalent to including a dummy per unit. Removes αᵢ but cannot estimate effects of time-invariant regressors.
- Random effects: assumes αᵢ uncorrelated with X; more efficient if true. The Hausman test compares FE and RE; rejection favours FE.
- Difference-in-differences is a two-period, two-group FE design; the key assumption is parallel trends. Card and Krueger (1994) on New Jersey's minimum wage is the classic example.
- Cluster standard errors by unit, because errors within a unit are correlated over time.

Time-series basics
- Stationarity: mean, variance and autocovariances do not change over time. Needed for standard inference.
- AR(1): Yₜ = c + ρYₜ₋₁ + εₜ is stationary if |ρ| < 1, with mean c/(1 − ρ) and variance σ²/(1 − ρ²).
- Random walk (ρ = 1): a unit root; shocks persist forever and variance grows with t. Difference it to get a stationary series.
- Augmented Dickey–Fuller test: H₀ is a unit root; it uses non-standard critical values.
- Spurious regression (Granger and Newbold, 1974): regressing one independent random walk on another often gives a high R² and "significant" t-statistics. Warning sign: high R² with a very low Durbin–Watson.
- Cointegration: two I(1) series whose linear combination is stationary share a long-run relationship (Engle and Granger, 1987); an error-correction model captures adjustment.
- Distributed lag models: the impact multiplier is the coefficient on Xₜ; the long-run multiplier is the sum of the lag coefficients.
- Granger causality tests whether past X improves forecasts of Y. It is predictive, not structural, causality.

Worked example
Yₜ = 1.5 + 0.7Yₜ₋₁ + εₜ has long-run mean 1.5/0.3 = 5. With σ² = 1, the variance is 1/(1 − 0.49) ≈ 1.96.

Exam pitfalls
- Using FE to estimate the effect of gender or other fixed traits (they are absorbed).
- Reading Granger causality as true causation.
- Running levels regressions on trending, non-stationary data without testing for unit roots or cointegration.

cards.f: Define the variance of a random variable X.
cards.b: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²], which equals E[X²] − (E[X])². It measures spread around the mean in squared units.

cards.f: What is Var(aX + bY)?
cards.b: a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y) + 2ab·Cov(X,Y). The covariance term vanishes only if X and Y are uncorrelated.

cards.f: Does zero covariance imply independence?
cards.b: No. Independence implies zero covariance, but not the reverse; for X symmetric about 0, X and X² are uncorrelated yet clearly dependent.

cards.f: State the law of iterated expectations.
cards.b: E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]]: averaging the conditional mean over the distribution of X gives the unconditional mean.

cards.f: Mean and variance of a Binomial(n, p)?
cards.b: Mean np, variance np(1 − p).

cards.f: What is special about the Poisson distribution's moments?
cards.b: Its mean and variance are both equal to λ.

cards.f: How is the t distribution constructed?
cards.b: t(k) = Z/√(V/k), where Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ²(k) are independent. It has fatter tails than the normal and tends to N(0,1) as k → ∞.

cards.f: What is an F(k₁, k₂) random variable?
cards.b: The ratio (V₁/k₁)/(V₂/k₂) of two independent chi-squared variables each divided by its degrees of freedom.

cards.f: A disease affects 1% of people. A test has 95% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate. P(disease | positive)?
cards.b: By Bayes' rule, 0.0095/(0.0095 + 0.0495) ≈ 0.16. Low prevalence means most positives are false.

cards.f: Can a probability density f(x) exceed 1?
cards.b: Yes. Only areas under f are probabilities, so f(x) can be above 1 on a narrow interval, e.g. Uniform(0, 0.5) has density 2.

cards.f: What makes an estimator unbiased?
cards.b: Its expected value equals the true parameter: E[θ̂] = θ.

cards.f: Why divide by n − 1 in the sample variance?
cards.b: Using X̄ in place of μ makes deviations systematically too small; dividing by n − 1 makes s² unbiased for σ².

cards.f: Decompose mean squared error.
cards.b: MSE(θ̂) = Var(θ̂) + [Bias(θ̂)]². A biased estimator can have lower MSE if it is much less variable.

cards.f: Define a consistent estimator.
cards.b: One that converges in probability to the true parameter as the sample size grows without bound.

cards.f: State the central limit theorem (i.i.d. case).
cards.b: If observations are i.i.d. with finite variance σ², √n(X̄ − μ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0,1), whatever the population's shape.

cards.f: Standard deviation vs standard error?
cards.b: Standard deviation describes spread in the data; standard error is the standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution, e.g. σ/√n for X̄.

cards.f: How much must n rise to halve the standard error of X̄?
cards.b: By a factor of four, because SE = σ/√n.

cards.f: What is maximum likelihood estimation?
cards.b: Choosing parameter values that maximise the probability (likelihood) of the observed data. Under regularity conditions it is consistent and asymptotically efficient.

cards.f: Is an unbiased estimator always consistent?
cards.b: No. E.g. using only the first observation X₁ to estimate μ is unbiased but never converges, because its variance does not shrink.

cards.f: Sample size needed to estimate a proportion within ±0.03 at 95% confidence (worst case)?
Define a Type I error.
cards.b: Rejecting a true null hypothesis. Its probability is the size of the test, α.

cards.f: Define statistical power.
cards.b: The probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false, i.e. 1 − P(Type II error).

cards.f: What exactly is a p-value?
cards.b: The probability, computed assuming H₀ is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not P(H₀ is true).

cards.f: General form of a t-statistic?
cards.b: (estimate − hypothesised value)/standard error of the estimate.

cards.f: Link between a two-sided 5% test and a 95% CI?
cards.b: H₀: θ = θ₀ is rejected at 5% exactly when θ₀ lies outside the 95% confidence interval.

cards.f: Correct frequentist interpretation of a 95% CI?
cards.b: If we repeated the sampling and built intervals the same way, 95% of them would contain the true parameter.

cards.f: What raises the power of a test?
cards.b: Larger sample size, larger true effect, less noise, and a larger α (at the cost of more Type I errors).

cards.f: Why say 'fail to reject' rather than 'accept' H₀?
cards.b: Non-rejection may reflect low power; the data are merely consistent with H₀, not proof of it.

cards.f: What is the multiple testing problem?
cards.b: Running many tests at 5% makes some false rejections likely by chance. Corrections such as Bonferroni (use α/m) control this.

cards.f: Statistical vs economic significance?
cards.b: Statistical significance concerns whether an effect is distinguishable from zero; economic significance concerns whether its size matters. Huge samples make tiny effects significant.

cards.f: Formula for the OLS slope in simple regression.
cards.b: β̂₁ = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)(Yᵢ − Ȳ)/Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)², the sample covariance of X and Y divided by the sample variance of X.

cards.f: Which point does the OLS line always pass through?
cards.b: The point of means (X̄, Ȳ), because β̂₀ = Ȳ − β̂₁X̄.

cards.f: Define R².
cards.b: R² = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS, the fraction of sample variation in Y explained by the regression.

cards.f: State the Gauss–Markov theorem.
cards.b: Under linearity, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean and homoskedasticity, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE).

cards.f: Which assumption is key for OLS to be unbiased?
cards.b: Zero conditional mean, E[u|X] = 0: the unobservables must be mean-independent of the regressor.

cards.f: Interpret β₁ in ln(Y) = β₀ + β₁X + u.
cards.b: A one-unit rise in X changes Y by approximately 100β₁ percent (exactly 100(e^β₁ − 1)%).

cards.f: Interpret β₁ in ln(Y) = β₀ + β₁ln(X) + u.
cards.b: β₁ is the elasticity of Y with respect to X: a 1% rise in X changes Y by about β₁%.

cards.f: Is normality of errors needed for OLS to be unbiased?
cards.b: No. Normality is only needed for exact small-sample t and F distributions; unbiasedness comes from E[u|X] = 0.

cards.f: Estimator of the error variance in simple regression?
cards.b: s² = RSS/(n − 2); two degrees of freedom are lost estimating β₀ and β₁.

cards.f: Why can't you test E[u|X] = 0 using OLS residuals?
cards.b: OLS forces residuals to be uncorrelated with X in the sample, so the residual-X correlation is zero by construction.

cards.f: Formula for omitted variable bias when X₂ is left out.
cards.b: E[β̃₁] = β₁ + β₂δ₁, where δ₁ is the slope from regressing X₂ on X₁.

cards.f: Direction of bias on returns to education if ability is omitted?
cards.b: Upward: ability raises wages and correlates positively with schooling, so β₂δ₁ > 0.

cards.f: What does the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem say?
cards.b: A multiple regression coefficient equals the slope from regressing Y on the part of that regressor left after partialling out the other regressors.

cards.f: Does high multicollinearity bias OLS?
cards.b: No. It leaves OLS unbiased but inflates the variances (standard errors) of the affected coefficients.

cards.f: Define the variance inflation factor.
cards.b: VIFⱼ = 1/(1 − Rⱼ²), where Rⱼ² comes from regressing Xⱼ on the other regressors.

cards.f: What is the dummy variable trap?
cards.b: Including a dummy for every category alongside an intercept creates perfect collinearity; drop one category as the base.

cards.f: Adjusted R² formula.
cards.b: R̄² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1); it can fall when a weak regressor is added.

cards.f: Marginal effect of X in Y = β₀ + β₁X + β₂X² + u?
cards.b: ∂Y/∂X = β₁ + 2β₂X, so it depends on X; the turning point is at X = −β₁/(2β₂).

cards.f: What is a 'bad control'?
cards.b: A variable that is itself an outcome of the treatment; controlling for it can introduce bias rather than remove it.

cards.f: Interpret the coefficient on D·X in Y = β₀ + β₁X + β₂D + β₃(D·X) + u.
cards.b: β₃ is the difference in the slope on X between the group with D = 1 and the base group.

cards.f: F-statistic for q linear restrictions (RSS form).
cards.b: F = [(RSSᵣ − RSSᵤ)/q]/[RSSᵤ/(n − k − 1)], compared with F(q, n − k − 1).

cards.f: Consequence of heteroskedasticity for OLS.
cards.b: Coefficients stay unbiased and consistent, but the usual standard errors are invalid and OLS is no longer BLUE.

cards.f: How does the Breusch–Pagan test work?
cards.b: Regress squared OLS residuals on the regressors; LM = nR² from that regression is approximately χ²(k) under homoskedasticity.

cards.f: Standard fix for heteroskedasticity of unknown form?
cards.b: Use heteroskedasticity-robust (White/Eicker–Huber) standard errors.

cards.f: Approximate relation between Durbin–Watson and ρ̂.
cards.b: DW ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂): about 2 means no first-order autocorrelation, near 0 strong positive, near 4 strong negative.

cards.f: Why use Breusch–Godfrey rather than Durbin–Watson?
cards.b: BG remains valid with lagged dependent variables and can test higher-order autocorrelation; DW is biased towards 2 when Yₜ₋₁ is a regressor.

cards.f: What do Newey–West standard errors correct for?
cards.b: Both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation (HAC) in the errors.

cards.f: What does the Jarque–Bera test check?
cards.b: Whether residuals are normal, using sample skewness and excess kurtosis.

cards.f: What is the Chow test for?
cards.b: Testing whether regression coefficients are equal across two subsamples, e.g. before and after a structural break.

cards.f: Can regressors be individually insignificant but jointly significant?
cards.b: Yes, often when they are highly correlated; use an F-test for joint significance.

cards.f: When is a regressor endogenous?
cards.b: When it is correlated with the error term, so E[u|X] ≠ 0 and OLS is biased and inconsistent.

cards.f: Three main sources of endogeneity.
cards.b: Omitted variables, measurement error in a regressor, and simultaneity (reverse causality).

cards.f: Effect of classical measurement error in X on OLS.
cards.b: It biases the slope towards zero (attenuation bias).

cards.f: Two conditions for a valid instrument Z.
cards.b: Relevance: Cov(Z, X) ≠ 0. Exogeneity: Cov(Z, u) = 0, so Z affects Y only through X.

cards.f: IV estimator with one instrument and one regressor.
cards.b: β̂_IV = Cov(Z, Y)/Cov(Z, X), i.e. the reduced-form coefficient divided by the first-stage coefficient.

cards.f: Why not run 2SLS by hand in two OLS steps?
cards.b: The second-stage standard errors use the wrong residuals (based on X̂, not X), so they are incorrect.

cards.f: What problems do weak instruments cause?
cards.b: 2SLS becomes biased towards OLS and its standard errors and tests become unreliable; a first-stage F below 10 is a common warning sign.

cards.f: What does a Sargan/Hansen overidentification test show?
cards.b: Whether multiple instruments give consistent estimates; rejection suggests at least one is invalid, but non-rejection does not prove validity.

cards.f: What is the LATE interpretation of IV?
cards.b: With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies the average effect for compliers, whose treatment status is changed by the instrument (Imbens and Angrist, 1994).

cards.f: Instrument used by Card (1995) for schooling?
cards.b: Growing up near a four-year college, which lowers the cost of further education.

cards.f: What does the fixed effects estimator remove?
cards.b: Any time-invariant unobserved individual effect αᵢ, by demeaning each variable within unit.

cards.f: Limitation of fixed effects.
cards.b: It cannot estimate coefficients on time-invariant regressors, and it uses only within-unit variation, which can be small and noisy.

cards.f: What does the Hausman test compare in panels?
cards.b: Fixed and random effects estimates. A significant difference suggests αᵢ is correlated with X, favouring FE.

cards.f: Key identifying assumption of difference-in-differences.
cards.b: Parallel trends: without treatment, the treated and control groups' outcomes would have moved in parallel.

cards.f: Define weak stationarity.
cards.b: A series with constant mean, constant variance and autocovariances that depend only on the lag, not on time.

cards.f: Mean of a stationary AR(1), Yₜ = c + ρYₜ₋₁ + εₜ?
cards.b: c/(1 − ρ), valid when |ρ| < 1.

cards.f: Null hypothesis of the (augmented) Dickey–Fuller test.
cards.b: The series has a unit root (is non-stationary).

cards.f: What is a spurious regression?
cards.b: A regression between independent non-stationary series that shows high R² and significant t-statistics by chance (Granger and Newbold, 1974).

cards.f: Define cointegration.
cards.b: Two I(1) series are cointegrated if some linear combination of them is stationary, implying a long-run equilibrium relationship.

cards.f: Does Granger causality establish causation?
cards.b: No. It shows that past X helps predict Y beyond Y's own past; it is about predictive content.

cards.f: Why cluster standard errors by unit in panel data?
cards.b: Errors for the same unit are usually correlated over time; ignoring this typically understates standard errors.

questions.q: If Var(X) = 4, what is Var(3 − 2X)?
questions.why: Adding a constant does not change variance and scaling by −2 multiplies it by (−2)² = 4, giving 16.

questions.q: Which statement about the central limit theorem is correct?
options: It implies that the population is normally distributed in large samples
It implies that the sample mean is approximately normal in large samples, whatever the population's shape (given finite variance)
It only applies when the population is already normal
It guarantees the sample mean is unbiased
questions.why: The CLT concerns the sampling distribution of X̄, not the data. Unbiasedness of X̄ holds anyway and is not what the CLT delivers.

questions.q: A Type II error is:
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.why: Type II is a missed effect: H₀ is false but we do not reject it. Its probability is 1 minus power.

questions.q: A two-sided test of H₀: μ = 10 gives p = 0.03. Which conclusion follows?
options: The probability that H₀ is true is 0.03
The 95% confidence interval for μ excludes 10
The 99% confidence interval for μ excludes 10
questions.why: By duality, rejection at 5% means 10 lies outside the 95% CI. Since p > 0.01, 10 lies inside the 99% CI.

questions.q: In the model ln(wage) = β₀ + β₁·educ + u, the estimate β̂₁ = 0.07 means that one more year of education is associated with:
questions.why: In a log–level model 100β₁ approximates the percentage change: about 7% (exactly e^0.07 − 1 ≈ 7.3%).

questions.q: True model: wage = β₀ + β₁·educ + β₂·ability + u with β₂ > 0. Ability is omitted and Corr(educ, ability) > 0. The OLS estimate of β₁ is:
options: Biased, but the sign cannot be determined
questions.why: Bias = β₂δ₁; both β₂ and the educ–ability association are positive, so the bias is positive.

questions.q: Heteroskedasticity in a cross-section regression means OLS coefficient estimates are:
options: Unbiased, but the usual standard errors are invalid
Unbiased and the usual standard errors remain valid
Biased, but the standard errors are valid
questions.why: Heteroskedasticity does not affect E[u|X] = 0, so OLS stays unbiased, but the conventional variance formula assumes constant variance.

questions.q: A time-series regression includes Yₜ₋₁ as a regressor. Which test for first-order autocorrelation is most appropriate?
questions.why: Durbin–Watson is biased towards 2 with a lagged dependent variable; Breusch–Godfrey remains valid.

questions.q: Classical measurement error in a single regressor X causes the OLS slope to be:
questions.why: Noise in X is correlated with the composite error, producing attenuation bias that does not vanish with n.

questions.q: A researcher estimates Yₜ = 0.4 + 0.9Xₜ for two independent random walks and finds R² = 0.85 and DW = 0.15. The most likely explanation is:
questions.why: High R² with a very low Durbin–Watson statistic is the classic signature of spurious regression (Granger and Newbold, 1974).

questions.q: Two assets have standard deviations 0.2 and 0.3 and correlation 0.5. Find the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio and comment.
markScheme: Uses Var = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂
Computes variance 0.0475
SD ≈ 0.218, below the average SD of 0.25, illustrating diversification
questions.modelAnswer: Variance = 0.25(0.04) + 0.25(0.09) + 2(0.25)(0.5)(0.2)(0.3) = 0.01 + 0.0225 + 0.015 = 0.0475. The standard deviation is √0.0475 ≈ 0.218. This is below the simple average of the two standard deviations (0.25) because the assets are imperfectly correlated, so some risk diversifies away.

questions.q: A poll of 600 voters finds 42% support for a policy. Compute a 95% confidence interval and state the assumption that justifies the normal approximation.
markScheme: Justified by the CLT with a large random sample
questions.modelAnswer: The estimated standard error is √(0.42 × 0.58/600) ≈ 0.0201. A 95% interval is 0.42 ± 1.96 × 0.0201 = 0.42 ± 0.039, about 38.1% to 45.9%. The normal approximation relies on the central limit theorem: with a large random sample, the sample proportion (a mean of Bernoulli variables) is approximately normal. It does not fix non-random sampling or non-response.

questions.q: Explain the difference between unbiasedness and consistency, giving an estimator that is unbiased but not consistent.
markScheme: Unbiased: E[θ̂] = θ at any fixed n
Consistent: θ̂ → θ in probability as n → ∞
Example: using only X₁ to estimate μ
Explains X₁ is unbiased but its variance σ² does not shrink
questions.modelAnswer: Unbiasedness is a fixed-sample property: the estimator's expected value equals the parameter. Consistency is asymptotic: the estimator collapses onto the true value as n grows. Using only the first observation, θ̂ = X₁, to estimate μ is unbiased since E[X₁] = μ, but its variance is σ² for every n, so it never concentrates around μ and is not consistent.

questions.q: Define the size and the power of a hypothesis test.
markScheme: Size: probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true (Type I error rate α)
Power: probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false (1 − P(Type II))
questions.modelAnswer: The size of a test is the probability of rejecting the null when the null is actually true, the Type I error rate, conventionally set at 5%. Power is the probability of correctly rejecting the null when it is false, which equals one minus the probability of a Type II error.

questions.q: Using X = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and Y = 9, 12, 14, 18, 19, 24, compute the OLS intercept and slope, and R² given RSS ≈ 3.14.
questions.modelAnswer: The means are X̄ = 35 and Ȳ = 16. The cross-product sum is 500 and Σ(X − X̄)² = 1750, so β̂₁ = 500/1750 = 2/7 ≈ 0.286 and β̂₀ = 16 − (2/7)(35) = 6. Deviations of Y from its mean are −7, −4, −2, 2, 3, 8, giving TSS = 146. With RSS = 22/7 ≈ 3.14, R² = 1 − 3.14/146 ≈ 0.978.

questions.q: Given R² = 0.40 from a regression with n = 50 and k = 4 regressors, compute adjusted R² and explain why it is reported.
markScheme: Formula R̄² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1)
R² never falls when regressors are added; R̄² penalises extra regressors
questions.modelAnswer: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − 0.40)(49/45) = 1 − 0.653 ≈ 0.347. Ordinary R² can only rise when a regressor is added, even an irrelevant one, so it rewards overfitting. The adjustment applies a degrees-of-freedom penalty, so R̄² falls if an added variable contributes too little explanatory power.

questions.q: In ln(wage) = β₀ + 0.03·exper − 0.0005·exper² + …, find the marginal effect of experience at 10 years and the turning point.
markScheme: Marginal effect = 0.03 − 2(0.0005)exper
At 10 years: 0.02, i.e. about 2% per extra year
Turning point exper = 0.03/(2 × 0.0005)
= 30 years
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiating, ∂ln(wage)/∂exper = 0.03 − 0.001·exper. At 10 years this is 0.03 − 0.01 = 0.02, so an extra year raises wages by about 2%. The effect is zero at exper = 0.03/0.001 = 30 years, after which the fitted profile slopes down. Treat the turning point with caution if few workers in the sample have that much experience.

questions.q: Explain how the Breusch–Pagan test for heteroskedasticity is carried out and how you would respond to a rejection.
markScheme: Estimate the model by OLS and save residuals
Regress û² on the regressors
LM = nR² compared with χ²(k)
If rejected, use robust standard errors (or WLS if the form is known)
questions.modelAnswer: Estimate the model by OLS and save the residuals. Regress the squared residuals on the original regressors. Under the null of homoskedasticity, the statistic nR² from this auxiliary regression is approximately χ²(k), where k is the number of regressors. A large value rejects homoskedasticity. The usual response is to keep the OLS coefficients but report heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, or use weighted least squares if the variance function is known.

questions.q: A study finds that living near a college raises log wages by 0.042 and raises schooling by 0.32 years. Compute the IV estimate of the return to schooling and state the two conditions it relies on.
markScheme: β̂_IV = reduced form/first stage
Relevance: proximity shifts schooling
Exclusion: proximity affects wages only through schooling
questions.modelAnswer: With one instrument, the IV estimate is the reduced-form effect divided by the first-stage effect: 0.042/0.32 ≈ 0.131, roughly a 13% return per year of schooling. This needs relevance, meaning proximity really shifts schooling, which the first stage can check. It also needs exogeneity, meaning proximity affects wages only through schooling and is unrelated to unobservables such as family background or local labour markets.

questions.q: Compare fixed effects and random effects estimators for panel data.
markScheme: FE removes αᵢ by within-unit demeaning, allowing correlation between αᵢ and X
RE assumes αᵢ uncorrelated with X, more efficient if true, can estimate time-invariant effects
Hausman test: significant difference favours FE
questions.modelAnswer: Fixed effects removes the unobserved individual effect by demeaning within each unit, so it stays consistent even if that effect is correlated with the regressors, but it cannot estimate coefficients on time-invariant variables. Random effects treats the individual effect as part of the error, assuming it is uncorrelated with the regressors. It is more efficient and keeps time-invariant variables if that assumption holds. A Hausman test compares the two; a significant difference favours FE.

questions.q: For Yₜ = 1.5 + 0.7Yₜ₋₁ + εₜ with Var(εₜ) = 1, find the long-run mean and variance, and explain what changes if the coefficient on Yₜ₋₁ were 1.
markScheme: With ρ = 1 the series has a unit root (random walk with drift)
No constant mean or variance; shocks persist; difference the series
questions.modelAnswer: Because |0.7| < 1 the process is stationary. Its mean is 1.5/(1 − 0.7) = 5 and its variance is 1/(1 − 0.7²) = 1/0.51 ≈ 1.96. With a coefficient of 1 the process becomes a random walk with drift. It has a unit root, its variance grows with time, its mean trends, and shocks never die out, so standard inference fails. You would test with Dickey–Fuller and model the first difference.

questions.q:
Ledgerline, a bank, screens transactions for fraud. 2% of transactions are fraudulent. Its detection model flags 90% of fraudulent transactions and wrongly flags 4% of legitimate ones.
(a) What proportion of all transactions is flagged? (3 marks)
(b) If a transaction is flagged, what is the probability it is fraudulent? (4 marks)
(c) Ledgerline adds a second, independent model with the same accuracy and investigates only transactions flagged by both. Find the probability of fraud given two flags, and comment on the trade-off. (5 marks)
markScheme: Correct statement of Bayes' rule
Comments that most flags are false positives because of the low base rate
Uses conditional independence: P(two flags | fraud) = 0.81, P(two flags | legit) = 0.0016
Notes the cost: only 81% of fraud now caught, so missed fraud rises from 10% to 19%
Notes the independence assumption may fail if both models use similar features
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) By the law of total probability, P(flag) = P(flag | fraud)P(fraud) + P(flag | legit)P(legit) = 0.9 × 0.02 + 0.04 × 0.98 = 0.018 + 0.0392 = 0.0572. So 5.72% of transactions are flagged.

(b) Bayes' rule gives P(fraud | flag) = 0.018/0.0572 ≈ 0.315. Only about 31% of flagged transactions are fraudulent. The test looks accurate, but fraud is rare, so the 4% false-positive rate applied to the large legitimate pool produces more false alarms (0.0392) than true detections (0.018). This is the base-rate effect.

(c) If the models are conditionally independent given the true status, P(two flags | fraud) = 0.9² = 0.81 and P(two flags | legit) = 0.04² = 0.0016. Then P(fraud and two flags) = 0.02 × 0.81 = 0.0162 and P(legit and two flags) = 0.98 × 0.0016 = 0.001568. The posterior is 0.0162/(0.0162 + 0.001568) ≈ 0.912.

Requiring both flags greatly improves precision: about 91% of investigated cases are now fraud, so investigators waste far less time. The cost is sensitivity. Only 81% of fraudulent transactions are flagged by both models, so the share of fraud missed rises from 10% to 19%. The right rule depends on the relative cost of a missed fraud versus a wasted investigation. The calculation also assumes the second model's errors are independent of the first's. If both rely on similar features, their mistakes will be positively correlated, and the posterior will be lower than 0.912.

questions.q:
Let X₁, …, Xₙ be i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ². Consider three estimators of μ:
W₁ = X̄; W₂ = (X₁ + Xₙ)/2; W₃ = nX̄/(n + 1).
(a) Find the bias and variance of each estimator. (6 marks)
(b) Find the MSE of W₃ and explain when it could beat X̄ on MSE. (4 marks)
(c) Which estimators are consistent? Justify your answers. (5 marks)
markScheme: W₁ unbiased, Var = σ²/n
W₂ unbiased, Var = σ²/2
W₃ bias = −μ/(n + 1)
Var(W₃) = nσ²/(n + 1)²
MSE(W₃) = [nσ² + μ²]/(n + 1)²
W₃ beats X̄ when μ² is small relative to σ² (μ² < σ²(2n + 1)/n)
W₁ consistent by the LLN / variance → 0
W₂ not consistent: variance fixed at σ²/2
W₃ consistent: bias and variance both → 0
Links to the bias–variance trade-off
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) W₁ = X̄ has E[X̄] = μ, so it is unbiased, and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.
W₂ averages two observations: E[W₂] = μ, so it is unbiased, and Var(W₂) = (σ² + σ²)/4 = σ²/2.
W₃ = (n/(n + 1))X̄ has E[W₃] = nμ/(n + 1), so its bias is nμ/(n + 1) − μ = −μ/(n + 1). Its variance is (n/(n + 1))² × σ²/n = nσ²/(n + 1)².

(b) MSE = variance + bias² = nσ²/(n + 1)² + μ²/(n + 1)² = (nσ² + μ²)/(n + 1)². Compare with MSE(X̄) = σ²/n. W₃ does better when (nσ² + μ²)/(n + 1)² < σ²/n. Rearranging, this holds when μ² < σ²(2n + 1)/n, roughly when μ² is less than about twice σ². Shrinking towards zero trades a little bias for lower variance. It helps when the true mean is small relative to the noise and hurts when μ is large. Because we do not know μ, this is a gamble, which is why shrinkage is mainly used where there is reason to expect parameters near zero.

(c) A sufficient condition for consistency is that bias and variance both go to zero as n → ∞. X̄ is consistent: it is unbiased, σ²/n → 0, and the law of large numbers applies. W₂ is unbiased but not consistent. Its variance stays at σ²/2 however large n is, because it ignores all but two observations. W₃ is consistent: its bias −μ/(n + 1) → 0 and its variance nσ²/(n + 1)² → 0. This shows that unbiasedness and consistency are separate properties. W₂ is unbiased but inconsistent, while W₃ is biased in finite samples but consistent.

questions.q:
A charity runs a numeracy programme. 64 pupils who took part score a mean of 72.5 on a test, with sample variance 64. A comparison group of 81 pupils scores a mean of 70.0, with sample variance 81.
(a) Test, at the 5% level, whether the programme changes mean scores (two-sided). (5 marks)
(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference and interpret it. (3 marks)
(c) The charity says a one-sided test is significant and the programme 'clearly works'. Evaluate this claim. (4 marks)
markScheme: States H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 and H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0
|t| < 1.96 (p ≈ 0.077), so fail to reject at 5%
Interval includes 0, consistent with the test
One-sided p ≈ 0.039 < 0.05, but the direction must be chosen before seeing data
Selection: participants not randomly assigned, so the difference may not be causal
Notes statistical vs practical significance / low power
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let μ₁ and μ₂ be the population means for participants and non-participants. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 against H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0. The difference in sample means is 72.5 − 70.0 = 2.5. Its standard error (unequal variances) is √(64/64 + 81/81) = √2 ≈ 1.414. The test statistic is t = 2.5/1.414 ≈ 1.77. With samples this large the critical value is close to 1.96. Since 1.77 < 1.96, we fail to reject H₀ at 5%; the two-sided p-value is about 0.077.

(b) The 95% interval is 2.5 ± 1.96 × 1.414 = 2.5 ± 2.77, about (−0.27, 5.27). Values from a small negative effect to an effect of about 5 points are consistent with the data. Because zero is inside the interval, this agrees with the test in (a). The interval is wide, which tells us the study is imprecise.

(c) A one-sided test of H₁: μ₁ > μ₂ gives p ≈ 0.039, which is below 0.05. That is only legitimate if the direction was specified before looking at the data. Switching to a one-sided test after seeing a two-sided p of 0.077 halves the p-value and inflates the real Type I error rate. More importantly, pupils were not randomly assigned. Families who sign up may be more motivated or better resourced, so the 2.5-point gap may reflect selection rather than the programme. Even if the effect is real, its size is modest and uncertain. 'Clearly works' overstates the evidence. A randomised trial, or controls for prior attainment, and a larger sample would be needed.

questions.q:
An analyst regresses monthly sales (Y, £000) on advertising spend (X, £000) for n = 25 months. Summary statistics: X̄ = 12, Ȳ = 40, Σ(X − X̄)² = 400, Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) = 600, Σ(Y − Ȳ)² = 1300.
(a) Compute the OLS slope and intercept. (3 marks)
(b) Compute R² and the standard error of the slope. (5 marks)
(c) Test H₀: β₁ = 1 against a two-sided alternative at 5%, and give a 95% CI for β₁. (4 marks)
(d) Predict sales when X = 15 and explain why the slope may not be a causal effect. (3 marks)
markScheme: ESS = β̂₁ × Σxy = 900 (or β̂₁² × Σx²)
t = (1.5 − 1)/0.209 ≈ 2.40 > t₂₃ critical 2.069, reject
Prediction 22 + 1.5 × 15 = 44.5
Causality: reverse causation / omitted factors such as seasonality affect both advertising and sales
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) β̂₁ = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ)/Σ(X − X̄)² = 600/400 = 1.5. β̂₀ = Ȳ − β̂₁X̄ = 40 − 1.5 × 12 = 22. Each extra £1,000 of advertising is associated with £1,500 more sales.

(b) The explained sum of squares is β̂₁² × Σ(X − X̄)² = 2.25 × 400 = 900. So RSS = 1300 − 900 = 400 and R² = 900/1300 ≈ 0.692: advertising accounts for about 69% of the sample variation in sales. The error variance estimate is s² = RSS/(n − 2) = 400/23 ≈ 17.39. So SE(β̂₁) = √(s²/Σ(X − X̄)²) = √(17.39/400) ≈ 0.209.

(c) t = (1.5 − 1)/0.209 ≈ 2.40. The 5% two-sided critical value from t with 23 degrees of freedom is about 2.069. Since 2.40 > 2.069, we reject H₀: β₁ = 1. The 95% CI is 1.5 ± 2.069 × 0.209 ≈ 1.5 ± 0.43, about (1.07, 1.93). It excludes 1, which agrees with the test, and it also excludes 0.

(d) Predicted sales = 22 + 1.5 × 15 = 44.5, i.e. £44,500. X = 15 is within the likely range of the data, so this is not a wild extrapolation.

The slope is a conditional association, not necessarily a causal effect. Firms often raise advertising when they expect strong demand, for example before Christmas, which creates reverse causality. Omitted factors such as seasonality, prices or competitor activity may drive both series. If any of these is correlated with X, then E[u|X] ≠ 0 and β̂₁ is biased. A high R² does not resolve this. Credible causal estimates would need controls for seasonality, an experiment such as randomised regional campaigns, or an instrument.

questions.q:
Using 400 workers, Priya estimates (standard errors in brackets):
ln(wage) = 1.20 + 0.080·educ + 0.030·exper − 0.0005·exper² + 0.120·union
(0.10) (0.012) (0.006) (0.0001) (0.040)
R² = 0.38.
(a) Interpret the coefficients on educ and union precisely. (4 marks)
(b) Find the marginal effect of experience at 10 years and the turning point. (3 marks)
(c) Compute adjusted R². (2 marks)
(d) Critically assess whether 0.080 is a credible estimate of the causal return to education. (7 marks)
markScheme: educ: one more year ≈ 8% higher wage, holding other regressors constant (exactly e^0.08 − 1 ≈ 8.3%)
union: e^0.12 − 1 ≈ 12.7% premium relative to non-members
Both significant (t ≈ 6.7 and 3)
Marginal effect of exper = 0.03 − 0.001·exper = 0.02 at 10 years
Turning point at 30 years
Omitted ability biases upwards (β₂ > 0, positive correlation)
Measurement error in educ attenuates the estimate
Union status may itself be endogenous / selection into unions
Solutions: IV (e.g. proximity, schooling laws), twin or sibling fixed effects, rich controls
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Holding experience and union status fixed, an extra year of education is associated with roughly 8% higher wages. The exact figure is e^0.08 − 1 ≈ 8.3%. The t-ratio is 0.080/0.012 ≈ 6.7, so it is highly significant. Union members earn about 12.7% more (e^0.12 − 1) than otherwise similar non-members, with t = 3.

(b) ∂ln(wage)/∂exper = 0.030 − 2(0.0005)exper = 0.030 − 0.001·exper. At 10 years this is 0.02, about 2% per extra year. The profile peaks at exper = 0.030/0.001 = 30 years. That is plausible, though the estimate beyond the peak depends on how many older workers are in the sample.

(c) With k = 4 regressors, R̄² = 1 − (1 − 0.38)(399/395) ≈ 1 − 0.62 × 1.0101 ≈ 0.374.

(d) The estimate is causal only if educ is uncorrelated with the error conditional on the controls. Several problems make that doubtful.
- Omitted ability or motivation probably raises both schooling and wages. The omitted variable bias formula, β₂δ₁ > 0, implies 0.080 overstates the true return.
- Family background works in the same direction.
- Measurement error in reported schooling attenuates the coefficient, pushing it towards zero, so the two biases partly offset.
- Heterogeneous returns matter too: people who expect high returns choose more schooling.
- The union dummy may itself be endogenous, because workers select into unionised jobs.

Better designs include IV using variation such as college proximity (Card, 1995) or compulsory schooling reforms, which identify a LATE. Within-twin or sibling fixed-effects comparisons remove shared family factors but magnify measurement error. Interestingly, many IV studies find returns similar to or above OLS, which suggests the biases may roughly cancel. Overall, 0.080 is a useful descriptive estimate but should not be read as a clean causal effect without a stronger identification strategy.

questions.q: 'Adding more control variables to a regression always makes the estimated effect of interest more credible.' Discuss with reference to multiple regression theory.
markScheme: Explains that controls reduce omitted variable bias when they are confounders (affect Y and correlate with X)
Uses the OVB formula β₂δ₁
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell: controls remove variation in X explained by them
Irrelevant controls do not bias but may reduce precision if correlated with X (multicollinearity, VIF)
Relevant controls uncorrelated with X can improve precision by reducing residual variance
Bad controls / mediators: controlling for outcomes of treatment changes the estimand or introduces selection bias
Colliders: conditioning on a common consequence creates spurious association
Controls cannot fix unobserved confounding, simultaneity or measurement error
Overfitting / specification searching and p-hacking concerns
Reaches a balanced conclusion: choose controls by causal reasoning, not quantity
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition contains a truth but overstates it. Whether a control helps depends on its causal role, not on how many controls are added.

Controls help when they are confounders. If X₂ affects Y and is correlated with X₁, omitting it biases β̂₁ by β₂δ₁. Including it removes that bias. By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, the coefficient on X₁ then uses only the variation in X₁ not explained by X₂, which is the ceteris paribus comparison we want. Adding a relevant variable that is uncorrelated with X₁ does not change the estimate's expected value, but it can shrink the residual variance and so the standard error.

Adding controls is not free, though. An irrelevant variable correlated with X₁ leaves OLS unbiased but inflates Var(β̂₁) through the VIF, making estimates less precise.

More seriously, some controls create bias. A 'bad control' is an outcome of the treatment. Suppose we estimate the effect of a degree on earnings and control for occupation. Part of the degree's effect works through occupation, so the coefficient no longer measures the total effect. It is also a comparison between selected groups who may differ in unobserved ability. Conditioning on a collider, a variable caused by both X and Y, can create a correlation where none exists. Controlling for a mediator changes the question being answered.

Controls also cannot fix problems that observables do not capture: unobserved confounders, simultaneity and measurement error remain. Adding variable after variable invites specification searching, where researchers keep the specification that gives significant results, and in small samples it can lead to overfitting. Stability of the coefficient as controls are added, as in Oster (2019), is informative but not proof.

In conclusion, credibility comes from a clear causal model that justifies each control (confounders in, mediators and colliders out), together with designs such as IV, panel fixed effects or experiments when key confounders are unobservable. More controls are not automatically better.

questions.q:
Tomasz estimates a model of household spending with n = 200 and k = 6 regressors, obtaining RSS = 1450. Dropping three regional variables gives RSS = 1540.
(a) Test the joint significance of the three regional variables at 5%. (5 marks)
(b) A Breusch–Pagan auxiliary regression of the squared residuals on the six regressors has R² = 0.06. Carry out the test. (4 marks)
(c) Explain the consequences of heteroskedasticity here and what Tomasz should do. (4 marks)
(d) Why might the three regional variables be jointly significant even if none is individually significant? (3 marks)
markScheme: H₀: the three coefficients are all zero
Critical F(3, 193) ≈ 2.65; reject H₀ (p ≈ 0.009)
Compare with χ²(6) 5% critical value 12.59: do not reject at 5% (p ≈ 0.062) but reject at 10%
Heteroskedasticity leaves OLS unbiased but invalidates the usual SEs and F-test
Use robust standard errors and a robust (Wald) joint test; WLS if form known
Joint significance with individual insignificance arises from correlation among regressors
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) H₀: the three regional coefficients are all zero. H₁: at least one is non-zero. The unrestricted model has n − k − 1 = 200 − 6 − 1 = 193 residual degrees of freedom. F = [(1540 − 1450)/3]/[1450/193] = 30/7.513 ≈ 3.99. The 5% critical value of F(3, 193) is about 2.65. Since 3.99 > 2.65, we reject H₀; the p-value is about 0.009. Region matters for spending once the other regressors are controlled for.

(b) The Breusch–Pagan LM statistic is nR² = 200 × 0.06 = 12. Under homoskedasticity it is approximately χ²(6), with a 5% critical value of 12.59. We narrowly fail to reject at 5% (p ≈ 0.062) but would reject at 10%. The evidence is borderline, not reassuring.

(c) If heteroskedasticity is present, the OLS coefficients are still unbiased and consistent, because Var(u|X) does not enter E[u|X]. But the conventional standard errors are wrong, so t-tests and the F-test in (a) can over- or under-reject, and OLS is no longer efficient. Given the borderline result, and because spending variance usually rises with income, Tomasz should report heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors as standard. He should also redo the joint test as a robust Wald test, since the RSS form of the F-test assumes homoskedasticity. If he can model the variance, for example as proportional to income, weighted least squares would be more efficient. Modelling log spending may also stabilise the variance.

(d) The regional dummies are likely to be correlated with one another and with other regressors. Multicollinearity inflates each individual standard error, so separate t-tests lack power. The F-test asks whether the group adds explanatory power, and it uses their combined contribution to reducing RSS. So a set of variables can matter together while no single coefficient is precisely estimated.

questions.q:
Northvale education authority caps classes at 30 pupils. If a school year has 31 pupils it must split into two classes, so enrolment just above 30 creates much smaller classes. Researchers using schools near the cutoff find:
- OLS: each extra pupil per class is associated with +0.10 points on a test (SE 0.03).
- First stage: crossing the cutoff reduces class size by 6.0 pupils (first-stage F = 45).
- Reduced form: crossing the cutoff raises test scores by 1.5 points.
(a) Compute the IV estimate and contrast it with OLS. (5 marks)
(b) Explain why OLS might be biased in this direction. (4 marks)
(c) Assess the relevance and exogeneity of the instrument. (7 marks)
(d) Interpret the estimate as a LATE and discuss external validity. (4 marks)
markScheme: β̂_IV = 1.5/(−6.0) = −0.25 points per extra pupil
Opposite sign to OLS: smaller classes raise scores
OLS biased upwards: weaker or disadvantaged pupils placed in smaller classes, or larger classes in popular/affluent schools
Relevance: first-stage F = 45 is well above the rule-of-thumb 10
Exclusion: crossing the cutoff should affect scores only via class size
Threats: manipulation of enrolment near cutoff (sorting), schools near cutoff differ, other resources tied to enrolment
Checks: density test at cutoff, balance of covariates, control for enrolment trend
Notes link to Angrist and Lavy (1999) Maimonides' rule design
LATE: effect for schools whose class size is shifted by the rule, near the cutoff
External validity to very different class sizes or settings is limited
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With one instrument, β̂_IV = reduced form/first stage = 1.5/(−6.0) = −0.25. Each extra pupil per class lowers test scores by 0.25 points, so cutting a class by 6 pupils raises scores by 1.5 points. OLS gives the opposite sign, +0.10.

(b) Class size is not randomly assigned. Head teachers often put weaker or disadvantaged pupils in smaller classes to give them more support. Popular, high-achieving schools in affluent areas tend to be oversubscribed and have larger classes. Both patterns make class size positively correlated with unobserved attainment factors in the error, so OLS is biased upwards.

(c) Relevance holds clearly. Crossing the cutoff cuts class size by 6 pupils, and the first-stage F of 45 is well above the conventional threshold of 10, so weak-instrument bias is not a concern. Exogeneity is the harder claim. The exclusion restriction requires that crossing the cutoff affects scores only through class size. The design follows the Maimonides' rule approach of Angrist and Lavy (1999) and compares schools just either side of the cutoff, where enrolment differences should be as good as random. Threats include:
- Manipulation: if parents or schools can push enrolment just over 30 to obtain smaller classes, the schools on each side differ systematically. A density test for bunching at 31 can check this.
- Enrolment itself may relate to school quality, so a smooth enrolment trend should be controlled for.
- Other resources, such as extra teachers or funding, may also be triggered by enrolment, which would violate exclusion.
Covariate balance checks on prior attainment and deprivation either side of the cutoff would strengthen the case.

(d) Under monotonicity, IV estimates a local average treatment effect: the effect of class size for schools whose classes are actually split because of the rule, and around class sizes near the cap (roughly 15 to 30). It need not apply to cutting classes from 20 to 10, to other age groups, or to systems with different teaching practices. Policy conclusions should be drawn with that limit in mind.

questions.q: 'Instrumental variables estimation solves the problem of endogeneity, so IV estimates should always be preferred to OLS.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines endogeneity and its sources (omitted variables, measurement error, simultaneity)
Explains IV conditions: relevance and exogeneity
IV consistent if conditions hold, while OLS inconsistent
IV has larger variance than OLS; bias–variance trade-off
Weak instruments: bias towards OLS, poor inference (Staiger and Stock, 1997; Bound, Jaeger and Baker, 1995)
Invalid instruments can produce inconsistency worse than OLS (bias scaled by 1/first stage)
Exclusion untestable; overidentification tests limited
LATE: IV estimates effect for compliers, may differ from the average effect
Hausman test to check whether OLS and IV differ
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Endogeneity, meaning correlation between a regressor and the error, arises from omitted variables, measurement error and simultaneity. It makes OLS biased and inconsistent. IV offers a way out: if Z is correlated with X (relevance) and uncorrelated with u (exogeneity), then β̂_IV = Cov(Z,Y)/Cov(Z,X) is consistent. In that sense IV can solve endogeneity. But the claim that IV should always be preferred fails on several counts.

First, IV is less precise. It uses only the variation in X induced by Z, so its variance exceeds that of OLS, sometimes by a lot. If the endogeneity is mild, OLS may have lower mean squared error. A Durbin–Wu–Hausman test can check whether the two estimates differ significantly.

Second, weak instruments. When Cov(Z,X) is small, 2SLS is biased towards OLS in finite samples, and conventional confidence intervals are misleading. Bound, Jaeger and Baker (1995) showed this for quarter-of-birth instruments, and Staiger and Stock (1997) proposed the first-stage F rule of thumb of 10. Weak-instrument-robust inference such as the Anderson–Rubin test helps but gives wide intervals.

Third, invalid instruments. The asymptotic bias of IV equals Corr(Z,u)/Corr(Z,X) scaled by relative standard deviations. A slightly invalid but weak instrument can therefore be more biased than OLS. Exclusion cannot be tested with a single instrument, and overidentification tests only check whether instruments agree with each other. They may all be invalid in the same direction.

Fourth, interpretation. With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies a LATE for compliers (Imbens and Angrist, 1994). That can differ from the average treatment effect that policy needs, and different instruments estimate different LATEs.

In conclusion, IV is a powerful tool when a strong instrument has a convincing exclusion argument, such as a natural experiment. It is not a mechanical improvement on OLS. The choice depends on instrument strength, credibility and the parameter of interest.

questions.q:
In 2024 the region of Eastmoor raised its minimum wage; neighbouring Westdale did not. Average employment per fast-food restaurant was:
Eastmoor: 20.0 before, 21.0 after. Westdale: 23.0 before, 21.5 after.
(a) Compute the difference-in-differences estimate. (3 marks)
(b) Write the regression that delivers this estimate and interpret each coefficient. (5 marks)
(c) State and assess the identifying assumption, and suggest checks. (5 marks)
(d) How should standard errors be computed? (2 marks)
markScheme: Eastmoor change +1.0; Westdale change −1.5
DiD = 1.0 − (−1.5) = +2.5 employees per restaurant
Regression Y = β₀ + β₁Treat + β₂Post + β₃(Treat × Post) + u
β₀ = Westdale before mean (23.0); β₁ = pre-period gap (−3.0)
β₂ = common time change from control (−1.5); β₃ = DiD effect (2.5)
Parallel trends assumption explained
Checks: pre-trends over several earlier periods / event study, placebo groups
Threats: region-specific shocks, spillovers, anticipation
Cluster standard errors at the regional or restaurant level; few clusters problem
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Eastmoor's employment rose by 21.0 − 20.0 = 1.0, while Westdale's fell by 21.5 − 23.0 = −1.5. The DiD estimate is 1.0 − (−1.5) = +2.5 employees per restaurant. Relative to the control, employment in the treated region rose after the minimum wage increase. This echoes the finding of Card and Krueger (1994) for New Jersey.

(b) Estimate Yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁Treatᵢ + β₂Postₜ + β₃(Treatᵢ × Postₜ) + uᵢₜ, where Treat = 1 for Eastmoor and Post = 1 after the change.
- β₀ = 23.0, the Westdale pre-period mean.
- β₁ = 20.0 − 23.0 = −3.0, the permanent pre-existing gap.
- β₂ = −1.5, the change over time common to both regions, measured in the control.
- β₃ = 2.5, the DiD treatment effect.
Restaurant fixed effects and time-varying controls can be added.

(c) The key assumption is parallel trends: without the policy, Eastmoor's employment would have changed by the same amount as Westdale's, −1.5. Level differences are allowed; different trends are not. Here Westdale fell sharply. If that reflects a Westdale-specific shock, such as a factory closure, the estimate overstates the effect. Checks include:
- plotting several pre-2024 periods to see whether the trends were parallel (an event-study design)
- placebo tests using a fake policy date or an unaffected sector such as higher-wage industries
- looking for anticipation effects and cross-border spillovers, for example workers commuting between regions.

(d) Observations within a region or restaurant are correlated over time and share common shocks, so standard errors should be clustered, at least by restaurant. With only two regions, region-level clustering is unreliable because there are too few clusters. This is a known limitation of two-group designs and argues for more control regions or methods such as synthetic control.

questions.q:
Using 60 years of annual data, Amara regresses log real consumption (cₜ) on log real income (yₜ) in levels: ĉₜ = 0.35 + 0.92yₜ, R² = 0.99, t = 75, Durbin–Watson = 0.21. Augmented Dickey–Fuller tests fail to reject a unit root for cₜ and yₜ but reject a unit root in their first differences. An ADF-type test on the residuals from the levels regression rejects a unit root at 5% (using Engle–Granger critical values).
Interpret these results and explain how Amara should model the relationship between consumption and income.
markScheme: Variables are I(1): non-stationary in levels, stationary in differences
Levels regression risks spurious regression (Granger and Newbold, 1974)
High R² with low DW is a warning sign; usual t-statistics invalid if not cointegrated
Residual unit-root test rejection implies cointegration (Engle and Granger, 1987)
Engle–Granger critical values differ from standard DF ones because residuals are estimated
With cointegration, levels estimate of 0.92 is a (super-)consistent long-run elasticity
But its standard errors are non-standard; t = 75 not directly usable
Recommends error-correction model: Δcₜ = α + γΔyₜ + λ(cₜ₋₁ − 0.35 − 0.92yₜ₋₁) + εₜ with λ < 0
Interprets γ as short-run effect, λ as speed of adjustment
Notes alternatives/limits: structural breaks, small sample power of ADF, Johansen approach
questions.modelAnswer:
The ADF results show that log consumption and log income are I(1): each has a unit root in levels but is stationary after first differencing. Regressing one I(1) variable on another is dangerous. Granger and Newbold (1974) showed that independent random walks regressed on each other routinely produce high R² values and huge t-statistics. An R² of 0.99 alongside a Durbin–Watson of 0.21 is exactly the pattern that suggests a spurious regression, because the residuals are highly persistent.

The residual test changes the picture. Rejecting a unit root in the residuals of the levels regression, using Engle–Granger critical values, implies that cₜ − 0.35 − 0.92yₜ is stationary. Engle–Granger values are needed because the residuals are estimated, which makes standard DF values too lenient. So consumption and income are cointegrated (Engle and Granger, 1987): they share a common stochastic trend and do not drift apart in the long run, as permanent-income theories predict.

Given cointegration, the levels estimate of 0.92 is a consistent, indeed super-consistent, estimate of the long-run income elasticity of consumption. However, the reported t-statistic of 75 has a non-standard distribution and serially correlated errors, so it cannot be used for conventional inference. Amara should use dynamic OLS or fully modified OLS for valid long-run inference.

Amara should estimate an error-correction model:
Δcₜ = α + γΔyₜ + λ(cₜ₋₁ − 0.35 − 0.92yₜ₋₁) + εₜ.
All terms are stationary, so standard inference applies. γ is the short-run effect of income growth on consumption growth. λ, expected to be negative, is the speed of adjustment: the fraction of last year's disequilibrium corrected each year. Lagged differences can be added to whiten the residuals.

Caveats: ADF tests have low power over 60 observations, structural breaks can mimic unit roots, and the Engle–Granger two-step approach handles only one cointegrating relation. The Johansen system method is an alternative when there are more variables.

questions.q: 'A result with p < 0.05 is a real finding.' Critically evaluate this claim with reference to the logic of hypothesis testing and the conduct of empirical research.
markScheme: Defines p-value correctly and states it is not P(H₀ true)
Notes 5% false-positive rate under true nulls by construction
Base rates and power: proportion of significant findings that are true depends on prior plausibility and power
Low power inflates effect sizes of significant results (winner's curse)
Multiple testing and p-hacking / researcher degrees of freedom
Publication bias distorts literature
Statistical vs economic significance; large n makes trivial effects significant
Significance says nothing about causality or model specification (OVB, endogeneity)
Remedies: pre-registration, replication, CIs and effect sizes, multiple testing corrections
Balanced conclusion: p < 0.05 is weak evidence against H₀, not proof
questions.modelAnswer:
A p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained. A result with p < 0.05 means the data would be unusual under the null. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the effect is real, and it is not the probability that H₀ is true. The claim mixes up these conditional probabilities.

First, false positives are built in. When the null is true, 5% of tests reject by construction. Whether a significant result is likely to be true depends on the prior plausibility of the hypothesis and the power of the test. Suppose only 10% of tested hypotheses are true and power is 50%. Among 1000 tests, there are 50 true positives and 45 false positives, so nearly half of the 'findings' are false.

Second, low power causes more than missed effects. Among underpowered studies, those that do reach significance tend to overstate the effect size, sometimes called the winner's curse.

Third, research practice. Researchers make many choices: which controls, which sample, which outcome, which functional form. Trying several and reporting the one with p < 0.05 inflates the true Type I error rate far above 5%. Publication bias compounds this, because journals favour significant results, so the published literature over-represents false positives. Replication projects in psychology and economics have found many significant results that do not reproduce.

Fourth, significance is not importance. With very large samples, economically trivial effects become significant, while important effects in small samples may not be. Confidence intervals and effect sizes convey more.

Fifth, significance says nothing about identification. A highly significant OLS coefficient can be badly biased by omitted variables or reverse causality.

Remedies include pre-registration and pre-analysis plans, replication, corrections for multiple testing (such as Bonferroni or false discovery rate methods), reporting confidence intervals, and stronger research designs. In conclusion, p < 0.05 is modest evidence against a specific null, conditional on the model being right. Treating it as proof of a real finding is a misreading.
